summary: Documents the values assigned from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations, such as protocol and port numbers. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1700.

eli5.summary: A giant list of agreed-upon numbers that computers use to say what kind of thing they are talking about. Everyone uses the same list so they understand each other.

questions: what is the assigned numbers rfc
subtitle: The 1992 master list of protocol numbers, port numbers, multicast groups and other values that Internet protocols agree on.

tldr.problem: Protocols need fixed numbers for things like the next-level protocol in an IP packet or the contact port of a service, and everyone has to use the same ones.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) hands out the values and this memo prints the current tables: version numbers, protocol numbers, well known and registered ports, multicast addresses, type-of-service values and many more.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1340 is Historic. It replaced RFC 1060 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 1700, and the memo says current information can be obtained from the IANA.

today: RFC 1340 is Historic: it was obsoleted by RFC 1700, and it had itself replaced RFC 1060. The memo itself says to ask the IANA for current assignments.

sections.title: What the Assigned Numbers Memo Is
sections.content:
RFC 1340 documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations. It says it will be updated periodically, and that current information can be obtained from the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

Anyone developing a protocol or application that needs a link, socket, port or protocol number is told to contact the IANA for an assignment. Most protocols listed are documented elsewhere in the RFC series, though some of the items are undocumented.

Each entry carries a bracketed reference such as [nn,iii]: the number cites a document and the letters cite the responsible person, using a NIC Ident where possible.
sections.eli5: When you invent a new game, you ask the person who keeps the rulebook for a number so nobody else picks the same one. That person is the IANA, and this memo is the list of numbers already handed out.

sections.title: Data Notation and Special Addresses
sections.content:
Numbers are written in decimal, and data is pictured in big-endian order: fields run left to right with the most significant octet on the left. When a multi-octet quantity is sent, the most significant octet goes first.

The memo also lists special IP address forms, written as network, subnet and host parts where -1 means all 1 bits. For example {0, 0} is this host on this network and may only be a source address, {-1, -1} is the limited broadcast and must never be forwarded outside the (sub-)net of the source, and {127, <any>} is the internal host loopback address that should never appear outside a host.

Class E addresses are reserved for experimental use, and a gateway not taking part in those experiments must ignore datagrams with a Class E destination.
sections.eli5: Numbers are written the way you read a page, biggest part first. Some addresses are special, like a shout to everyone on your street or a note you leave for yourself.

sections.title: Version, Protocol and Port Numbers
sections.content:
The IP version field is 4 bits wide; value 4 is IP and 5 is ST Datagram Mode. The IP protocol field is 8 bits and names the next-level protocol. Examples in the table are 1 for ICMP, 6 for TCP and 17 for UDP, with 99 to 254 unassigned.

Well known ports are controlled and assigned by the IANA, and on most systems can only be used by system (or root) processes or privileged users. The assigned range used to be 0 to 255 and had been expanded to 0 to 1023. Each service has a contact port, and the same assignment is used for TCP and UDP where possible. Examples include 21 for FTP, 23 for Telnet, 25 for SMTP, 53 for the domain name server, 80 for www and 161 for SNMP.

Registered ports are in the range 1024 to 65535. The IANA does not control their use; it registers or lists them as a convenience, and on most systems ordinary user processes can use them.
sections.eli5: A computer can run many services at once, like a building with many doors. Each service listens at its own numbered door, and the famous doors have the same number everywhere so visitors know where to knock.

sections.title: Multicast Addresses and the IANA Ethernet Block
sections.content:
The memo lists Internet multicast addresses in use. 224.0.0.1 means all systems on this subnet and 224.0.0.2 all routers on this subnet; other entries cover OSPFIGP, RIP2 routers, NTP (224.0.1.1) and more. Ranges such as 224.2.0.0 to 224.2.255.255 are listed for multimedia conference calls.

On an Ethernet or IEEE 802 network, the 23 low-order bits of the IP multicast address go into the low-order 23 bits of the multicast hardware address. The IANA owns an Ethernet address block, and the Internet multicast range is 01-00-5E-00-00-00 to 01-00-5E-7F-FF-FF in hex.
sections.eli5: Multicast is like a group chat: instead of writing to one friend you send one message that everyone in the group gets. The list says which group name means which crowd.

sections.title: Type of Service, Time to Live and Other Parameters
sections.content:
There are four assigned type-of-service (TOS) values: low delay, high throughput, high reliability and low cost. Only one can be requested in any one IP datagram. Recommended values include 1000 (minimize delay) for TELNET, 0100 (maximize throughput) for FTP data and 0010 (maximize reliability) for SNMP.

The recommended default IP time to live (TTL) is 64.

The memo then continues with many other tables: DNS classes and types, BOOTP and network management parameters, Ethernet and IEEE 802 numbers, PPP fields, ARP parameters, Telnet options, MIME types, character sets, machine, system, protocol and terminal type names, a list of documents and a list of people.
sections.eli5: Some packets are in a hurry and some are heavy. A small label tells the network which kind each one is, and a countdown number keeps lost packets from wandering forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that security issues are not discussed in it. It is a registry of values, not a protocol, so it defines no behavior of its own beyond recording these assignments.
sections.eli5: This is only a list of numbers, so it does not talk about keeping secrets safe.
